protocol.legal_basis: Authorisation page (p2): 'Community Pharmacy Expanded Scope of Practice Initiative. In accordance with regulation 17A of the Controlled Substances (Poisons) Regulations 2011 (the Poisons Regulations) a pharmacist is authorised to prescribe a prescription drug (not being a drug of dependence) if the pharmacist is included on the register of authorised pharmacists and the drug is prescribed in accordance with the Community Pharmacist Prescribing Code.'
protocol.supervision_model: Document does not use 'collaborative'/'autonomous' terminology; its own wording: an authorised pharmacist on the register of authorised pharmacists prescribing in accordance with the Community Pharmacist Prescribing Code (p2), plus an explicit capability requirement (p12): 'Pharmacists must ensure that they have received additional adequate training, supervision and experience, and possess confidence in suturing / wound closure prior to provision under this Service.' Discretion clause (p7): 'When applying the information contained within this clinical practice guideline, pharmacists are advised to exercise professional discretion and judgement. The clinical practice guideline does not override the responsibility of the pharmacist to make decisions appropriate to the circumstances of the individual, in consultation with the patient and/or their carer.'
protocol.scope_summary: SA Health (Community Pharmacy Expanded Scope of Practice Initiative) clinical practice guideline for pharmacist assessment and management of an acute minor wound (caused by injury or trauma, epidermis/upper dermis or dermis, inflammation stage approximately 0-4 days post injury). Service restricted to patients aged 5 years or over. Covers 'Red flag' warning signs necessitating referral to emergency medical care (burns per ANZBA criteria; immediate referral to an emergency department – call 000; immediate referral via private vehicle; urgent referral within 24 hours to a general practitioner or Urgent Care Centre), 'Treat (if clinically appropriate) and concurrently refer' situations, key points (topical antibiotics not included in the Service; antibiotic prophylaxis not routinely recommended), comprehensive wound assessment (Table 1), pathology testing criteria, management (local anaesthetic, wound cleansing, wound closure, wound dressing, pharmacotherapy including antibiotics and tetanus post-exposure prophylaxis), confirmation of management, communication of the agreed management plan, general advice, clinical review and resources. 'Ineligibility for treatment as part of a prescribing service does not preclude a patient from accessing services provided as part of usual pharmacy care.'

diagnosis_pathways.name: Assessment and management of an acute minor wound

steps.description: Gather information and assess patient's needs: 'A comprehensive and holistic wound assessment must consider both patient and wound history (2, 8-10).' Patient history (p8-p9): 'Sufficient information should be obtained from the patient to assess the safety and appropriateness of any recommendations and medicines.' Consider: age; pregnancy and breastfeeding status (if applicable); mechanism of injury – 'immediate referral to ED if concern for potential blood borne virus exposure, e.g., needlestick injury, human bite; or if secondary injury is high risk, e.g., head injury, inhalation injury for burns'; patient weight (if local anaesthesia is required); current medical conditions, particularly conditions that may increase risk of infection (immunocompromised) or impair wound healing (e.g., vascular disease, diabetes mellitus, autoimmune disorders, malignancy); factors that may impact on successful wound healing as per the Therapeutic Guidelines: Factors affecting ulcer and wound healing (12); symptoms that may indicate systemic infection or other injury including fever, lymphadenopathy, nausea and vomiting; current, recently commenced or recently ceased medicines (including prescribed medicines, vitamins, herbs, other supplements and over-the-counter medicines), including medicines that may delay wound healing; previous healing and scarring experiences; allergies/adverse drug reactions; alcohol and drug history; smoking/vaping status; immunisation status including tetanus vaccination; risk factors for infection with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA); psychosocial history, emotional and mental state including level of distress, history of mental health conditions and potential for family violence; ability to undertake appropriate self-care; nutritional and hydration status. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients: 'Consider referring to the CARPA Standard Treatment Manual for further information for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients living in rural and remote communities (15).' Reminder: 'Pharmacists can access a range of clinical information in a patient's My Health Record, including details about current and past medication history, allergies and current medical conditions.' Wound history (p9): Consider mechanism of injury (other injuries that may require medical attention e.g., head injuries, bone fractures, human bites, needlestick injuries, animal bites, scratches or envenomation; potential for retained foreign bodies); date and time of injury; environment where the wound was acquired e.g., fresh or salt water, muddy locations, contaminated soil; treatments already provided and response e.g., dressings, antiseptics, antibiotics; whether the injury was sustained in a workplace or related to employment; whether the injury is a result of a dog bite ('South Australia requires the mandatory reporting of dog bites and attacks to the local council where the incident occurred'); injury/ies that may be associated with family violence or self-harm. Family violence (p9-p10): 'Indications of injuries associated with family violence may include injuries and/or bruising to the head, neck, face, areas usually hidden from view, bite marks, unusual burns, injuries that do not match the history/explanation given by the patient (or parent/caregiver) or no explanation can be provided (18).' 'If the pharmacist suspects the patient has been subjected to family violence, they should provide appropriate support and assistance to the patient (separate from other family members), including referral to support options.' 'Pharmacists must report suspected child abuse and neglect to Child Safety.' Self-harm (p10): 'Pharmacist assessment of a patient presenting with self-inflicted injuries, or a suspected self-inflicted injury, should consider: the patient's emotional and mental state and level of distress; whether there is an immediate concern related to the patient's safety; the need for referral to a mental health service (23).' 'Self-harm may be a repetitive behaviour (21).' 'Self-inflicted injuries are a warning sign that indicate a patient might be at a heightened risk of suicide. Consider key questions and/or other risk factors for suicide risk in accordance with the Therapeutic Guidelines - Suicide Risk (24).' Helplines listed (p10): Beyond Blue (1300 224 636); e-headspace (1800 650 890); Kids Helpline (1800 551 800); Lifeline (13 1114); Suicide Call Back Service (1300 659 467) (24).

steps.description: Confirm the presentation is an acute minor wound within the Service: 'An acute minor wound is defined as a wound: caused by injury or trauma (as opposed to surgical wounds); involving the epidermis and upper dermis (superficial) or dermis (partial) (9); in the inflammation stage (approximately 0-4 days post injury) and expected to follow the normal physiological wound healing process.' Key points (p7): 'Comprehensive assessment that includes wound, patient and environmental factors is required to determine appropriate management, including whether referral to a medical practitioner is required.' 'Wound healing is optimised when the wound is cleansed to remove debris and devitalised tissue, kept moist, infection is prevented, and the wound has adequate blood supply (2).'

gates.criterion: wound caused by injury or trauma, not a surgical wound (INC-2)

wound involves the epidermis and upper dermis (superficial) or dermis (partial), not full thickness — 'The wound is suspected to be full thickness (involving epidermis, dermis and subcutaneous tissue)' requires immediate referral to an emergency department (EXC-25 / RF-26)
wound in the inflammation stage (approximately 0-4 days post injury) and expected to follow the normal physiological wound healing process (INC-4)
wound history is clear — how, where and when the wound was acquired ('The wound history is unclear' requires urgent referral within 24 hours, EXC-34 / RF-35)
wound is not a skin tear, surgical/chronic wound infection, or a wound showing abnormal signs of healing (EXC-29, EXC-32, EXC-35 / RF-30, RF-33, RF-36)

wound is not significantly contaminated (foreign body or contamination that cannot be removed by the pharmacist, or significantly contaminated water-immersed wound) — treat and concurrently refer (EXC-36 / RF-37)

steps.description: Assessment and examination: 'Wound-related factors to be considered and documented during initial clinical assessment and at clinical review (if applicable) are detailed in Table 1.' Table 1. Clinical acute wound assessment (2, 6, 8, 9, 25): Anatomical location — 'Consider possible damage to joint, tendon, nerve and vascular structures'; 'Check distal sensation, motor function, range of motion (extensors and flexors) and vascularity.' Size and degree of tissue loss — 'Length, circumference and width'; 'Approximate depth - measured with a damp cotton tip, although generally not required for a minor acute wound'; 'Tissue loss - superficial, partial or full thickness.' Wound appearance — 'Presence of wound contamination - consider if the wound can be adequately cleaned, including with simple debridement, in the community pharmacy setting, or if referral is required'; 'Stage/phase of healing - inflammation, reconstruction/proliferation, maturation'; 'Wound bed clinical appearance (if visible) - granulation tissue, epithelial tissue, sloughy, necrotic, hyper-granulation tissue'; 'Wound edges and surrounding skin (colour, contraction, change in sensation) - signs of normal or abnormal healing'; 'Exudate - type, amount, colour and odour.' Signs of infection — 'Local infection - redness, heat, pain and swelling above normal inflammatory responses, presence of exudate, odour, impaired wound healing, contact bleeding, tissue breakdown, unhealthy granulation tissue'; 'Spreading infection - increasing wound size, lymphangitis, inflammation and swelling of lymph nodes, wound breakdown, patient malaise or deterioration in health'; 'Systemic infection - fever, tachycardia, hypotension, other signs of sepsis'. Pain — 'Timing, triggers, severity and impact'; 'Type of pain - background, breakthrough pain, precipitating factors, pain before during and/or after dressing, cleaning and exposure to air'; 'Response to any medication used to manage wound.' 'Conduct assessment of vital signs (including temperature, HR and BP) for any patients presenting with signs of infection in Table 1.' The TIME acronym (Tissue, Infection/Inflammation, Moisture balance, Edge and peri-wound area) 'as detailed in the Therapeutic Guidelines: Fundamentals of ulcer and wound management may also be used to guide wound examination and documentation of characteristics (3).' 'Consider SA Health Alerts for local outbreaks that may impact wounds and affect patient management.'

anatomical location assessed: no possible damage to joint, tendon, nerve and vascular structures — 'Injury with suspected vascular, tendon, joint, bone, muscle, or nerve involvement' requires immediate referral to an emergency department, call 000 (EXC-14 / RF-15)

tissue loss is superficial or partial, not full thickness (EXC-25 / RF-26)

steps.description: Pathology testing for Gram stain, culture and sensitivity testing: 'Pathology testing for Gram stain, culture and sensitivity testing, with referral to a medical practitioner for ongoing management is required for: spreading infection; infections resulting from penetrating wounds through footwear; water-immersed wounds; bites/clenched-fist injuries (referral to ED as post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) / Hepatitis B immunoglobulin may be warranted).' 'The patient must be advised to commence antibiotic therapy only after specimen collection has been completed.' (p12)

gates.criterion: spreading infection, infection from a penetrating wound through footwear, water-immersed wound, or bites/clenched-fist injuries → pathology testing for Gram stain, culture and sensitivity arranged WITH referral to a medical practitioner for ongoing management
specimen collection completed before antibiotic therapy is commenced — 'The patient must be advised to commence antibiotic therapy only after specimen collection has been completed.'
bites/clenched-fist injuries: consideration of referral to ED as post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) / Hepatitis B immunoglobulin may be warranted

steps.description: Red-flag triage: ''Red flag' warning signs at patient presentation that necessitate referral to emergency medical care' (p4-p5). (a) 'Provide first aid and concurrent immediate referral to an emergency department in the following situations' — burns beyond minor burns per ANZBA Criteria (1); 'The following require an immediate referral to an emergency department – call 000:' burns greater than 10% TBSA in adults; burns greater than 5% TBSA in children; burns of special areas - face, hands, feet, genitalia, perineum, major joints and circumferential limb or chest burns; burns with inhalation injury; electrical burns; chemical burns; burns associated with major trauma; non-accidental burns (consider ambulance vs private vehicle depending on patient safety, but low threshold to call ambulance). 'The following require an immediate referral to an emergency department – can occur via private vehicle (unless clinical assessment is concerning and warrants ambulance transfer):' full thickness burns; burns with pre-existing illness; burns at the extremes of age - young children and the elderly; burn injury in pregnant women (1). (b) p5 'Provide first aid and concurrent immediate referral to an emergency department - call 000:' injury with suspected vascular, tendon, joint, bone, muscle, or nerve involvement; fractures, crush injuries, partial amputations of a digit or potentially penetrating wounds of the torso; penetrating wound through footwear, a marine envenomation or other penetrating injury (a complex wound at high risk of infection); suspected concussive head injury. (c) p5 private-vehicle group: recent orofacial trauma (not yet seen by a dental practitioner); pain that requires management with treatments not available to pharmacists; needlestick injury; laceration to genitals; signs/symptoms of systemic infection or generally unwell; tetanus prone wound requiring tetanus immunoglobulin (e.g. less than 3 doses of the tetanus toxoid vaccine, or vaccination history is unknown); significant risk of suicide or self-inflicted injuries (see 'Treat and concurrently refer') – consider calling 000 if concerned about acute risk; wound suspected to be full thickness (involving epidermis, dermis and subcutaneous tissue); wound to the head (scalp, face, ears, eyes) or neck, or where sustained closure is difficult to achieve; anaesthesia (if indicated) cannot be achieved for adequate cleansing or closure. (d) p6 'Refer to a general practitioner or Urgent Care Centre: Urgent referral within 24 hours:' eight triggers (EXC-28 to EXC-35). (e) p7 'Treat (if clinically appropriate) and concurrently refer' situations (EXC-36 to EXC-38) proceed to PW-1-S6 with concurrent referral. See RF-1 to RF-50.

steps.description: Management and treatment plan (p12-p14): 'Pharmacists must ensure that they have received additional adequate training, supervision and experience, and possess confidence in suturing / wound closure prior to provision under this Service.' 'Pharmacist management of acute minor wounds may involve:' administration of local anaesthetic — 'Use of 1% lidocaine (without adrenaline, maximum of 10ml) if required, in accordance with the: Therapeutic Guidelines: Pain and analgesia (local anaesthetics for acute pain management) (26); Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for local anaesthesia (27); Queensland Health and Royal Flying Doctor Service (Queensland Section) Primary Clinical Care Manual (6).' wound cleansing — 'Irrigation, simple mechanical debridement (using sterile gauze) and use of antiseptics (if required) in accordance with the: Therapeutic Guidelines: Fundamentals of ulcer and wound management (3); Queensland Health and Royal Flying Doctor Service (Queensland Section) Primary Clinical Care Manual (6).' wound closure — 'Closure using topical skin/tissue adhesives and basic suturing techniques (if required and appropriate) in accordance with the: Therapeutic Guidelines: Fundamentals of ulcer and wound management (3); Queensland Health and Royal Flying Doctor Service (Queensland Section) Primary al Care Manual (6).' open_questions.topic: No specific antibiotic agent, strength, dose, route, frequency or duration printed (delegated to Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
open_questions.observed: Three antibiotic therapy rows (TX-5 presumptive, TX-6 prophylactic, TX-7 empirical) name only the indication and the Therapeutic Guidelines section. Route recorded as 'oral' is an inference from 'antibiotic therapy', not printed wording.
open_questions.why_unclear: The document names no agent, strength, dose, frequency or duration; inventing them would breach the never-invent rule. Route should be confirmed against the referenced Therapeutic Guidelines sections.

open_questions.topic: Tetanus immunoglobulin trigger is compound: numeric branch AND unknown-history branch
open_questions.observed: 'The patient has a tetanus prone wound and requires tetanus immunoglobulin (e.g. patient has had less than 3 doses of the tetanus toxoid vaccine, or vaccination history is unknown)' (p5).
open_questions.why_unclear: RF-24 structured captures only the numeric branch ({tetanus_toxoid_doses} < 3 doses); the 'vaccination history is unknown' branch has no numeric form and must be evaluated from trigger_text.

open_questions.topic: Same 4-day epithelialisation threshold carries two different escalation levels
open_questions.observed: p6: 'wounds older than 4 days that have not begun epithelialisation' is an 'Urgent referral within 24 hours' trigger to a general practitioner or Urgent Care Centre (RF-36, structured > 4 days). p14: 'the wound is not healing as expected (e.g. no evidence of epithelialisation 4 days post wound event)' is general advice to see an appropriate healthcare provider (RF-48, structured >= 4 days).
open_questions.why_unclear: Both readings recorded as printed; the engine must decide which tier applies at exactly 4 days and thereafter (>= vs >).

open_questions.observed: Inclusion uses all_of (INC-1 to INC-6) and exclusion uses any_of (EXC-1 to EXC-35 for the referral tiers; EXC-36 to EXC-38 for treat-and-concurrently-refer); the document never prints an AND/OR key but states each red flag 'necessitate[s] referral'.
open_questions.why_unclear: Combinatorics derived from wording rather than stated; recorded here per spec rule 4.

open_questions.topic: Mapping of the document's own urgency tiers to action/severity
open_questions.observed: 'Immediate referral to an emergency department – call 000' → ESCALATE_000 / critical; 'immediate referral to an emergency department – can occur via private vehicle' → REFER_URGENT / critical; 'Urgent referral within 24 hours' (GP or Urgent Care Centre) → REFER_URGENT / high; 'Treat (if clinically appropriate) and concurrently refer' → REFER / medium; general advice 'see an appropriate healthcare provider' → REVIEW_GP / medium; treatment prohibition (topical antibiotics) → NOT_ELIGIBLE / low.
open_questions.why_unclear: The document prints its own tiers but no numeric severity; mapping recorded so it can be re-checked. Note the private-vehicle group is still worded 'immediate referral to an emergency department'.
